title: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (4 of 7)
hook: a monk burns two birds with a look, and a woman at a door tells him to wait
tomorrow: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (5 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the birds who fed a guest. Each is great in its own place, the householder too.
screen: `EACH IS GREAT IN ITS OWN PLACE.`

segments.voice: A young monk goes into the forest and meditates for years. He gets good at it. Maybe too good. One day a crow and a crane start fighting in the branches above him, and dry leaves fall on his head. He looks up, furious, and a flash of fire leaves his eyes. The two birds fall to the ground, burned. He's thrilled: I can burn birds with a look. Then he gets hungry, walks into town, and knocks on a door to beg for food. From inside, a woman calls out: wait a little, my son. He's about to learn something the forest never taught him.
screen: `A MONK WHO BURNED TWO BIRDS.` → `A DOOR IN TOWN.` → `WAIT A LITTLE, MY SON.`

segments.voice: Vivekananda tells this story in the Karma Yoga lecture called What Is Duty? The monk stands at the door, fuming. How dare she make me wait. Doesn't she know what I can do? From inside, the woman says: don't think so much of yourself. There's no crow or crane here. He's stunned. How did she know? When she finally comes out, she explains. Her husband was ill, and she was caring for him. That was her duty, done with her whole heart, and it was all her practice. Through it, the story says, she had come to see more than his years in the forest had shown him. Then she sends him on: go to the market and find the butcher. He'll teach you. The monk is shocked: a butcher, of all people, his teacher? He goes anyway. The butcher, cutting meat, looks up: the lady sent you? Sit down, wait until I've finished. He takes the monk home, washes and feeds his old parents first, and only then sits down to teach him. What he teaches is a whole section of the Mahabharata, the Vyadha Gita, the song of the hunter-butcher. Vivekananda's point is sharp. The woman and the butcher were not saints by job title. They did the duty in front of them, without selfishness, with care. Work done like that, he says, is worship. Fire from the eyes is not the goal.
screen: `NO CROW OR CRANE HERE.` · `SHE WAS CARING FOR HER HUSBAND.` · `THE BUTCHER WHO FED HIS PARENTS FIRST.` · `DUTY, DONE WITH CARE, IS WORSHIP.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind whoever made you wait most recently, the pharmacy line, a kid who needed one more thing, a parent on the phone, and notice the flash of heat without pushing it away. Then picture the woman at the door, doing what was in front of her. Breathe in and let the waiting be part of the work; breathe out and let the heat cool.
Vyadha, a hunter, the butcher who taught the monk. The duty in front of you, done without selfishness and with care, is already the practice.
Your line: offer the work. Whoever keeps you waiting might be caring for someone. Day two hundred sixty-three, complete.

howItsDone: Many Hindus understand caring for parents, spouse and children as dharma and as a form of worship, and the Vyadha Gita, the butcher's teaching in the Mahabharata, is often cited to show that holiness isn't tied to a particular job.

original.note: Sanskrit: vyadha, a hunter; in this story the dharma-vyadha, the righteous hunter-butcher of the Mahabharata.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy people are the ones who leave everything and meditate.
what it means: in karma yoga, a wife at a sickbed and a butcher at his counter can be further along than a monk.

what a scholar hears: Vivekananda draws on the Mahabharata's Vana Parva, where a proud brahmin is humbled by a devoted wife and sent to the dharma-vyadha in Mithila; the vyadha's teaching is known as the Vyadha Gita.
